claims.text: The starting material is pre-exposure Q235 carbon steel in its native, untreated surface state.
A thin, uniform phosphonate inhibitor film can be deposited on Q235 steel by solution-based self-assembly.
The phosphonate film suppresses anodic dissolution by modifying the local electrochemical environment at the Q235 steel surface.
Film integrity controls the onset or suppression of Q235 corrosion degradation in chloride solution at room temperature and 80°C.
The governing structural mediator consists of the integrity, thickness, and chemical state of the phosphonate film at the steel/electrolyte interface.
Adsorbed phosphonate groups form a cohesive barrier against electrochemical attack.
The phosphonate barrier reduces electron-transfer rates and thereby lowers the rate of anodic dissolution.
At elevated temperature, degradation or loss of cohesion of the phosphonate film causes electrochemical protection to fail and corrosion to accelerate.
Phosphonate-treated Q235 samples will have lower corrosion current density than untreated samples at room temperature and 80°C.
Phosphonate-treated Q235 samples will have higher polarization resistance than untreated samples at room temperature and 80°C.
Phosphonate-treated Q235 samples will exhibit less corrosion-related mass loss than untreated samples.
Loss of monitored film integrity will be followed by a rapid increase in corrosion rate comparable to that of the intentionally disrupted-film group.
Open-circuit potential, potentiodynamic polarization, corrosion current density, and polarization resistance are applicable electrochemical measures in 3.5 wt.% NaCl at room temperature.
In situ XPS or IR spectroscopy can monitor phosphonate-film thickness, integrity, and chemical state during corrosion testing in aqueous NaCl at room temperature and 80°C.
Elevated-temperature stability and adherence of the phosphonate inhibitor film are known challenges.
An intact phosphonate film without improved corrosion resistance would falsify the proposed film-protection mechanism.
